question: The European game industry is one of the EU’s fastest-growing cultural sectors, generating significant innovation, exports and jobs across Member States. With 5 900 game studios in the EU, the combined industry turnover was EUR 18.7 billion in 2023. However, European game developers increasingly face global competition from regions with lighter and more predictable regulatory environments.

The Digital Fairness Act1 aims to strengthen consumer protection and ensure fair digital markets. While these objectives are important, there is concern that new compliance obligations could further burden smaller European game studios and start-ups, reducing their competitiveness vis-à-vis global actors.
At the same time planned simplification measures are insufficient considering the new regulatory burden facing these studios. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the Digital Fairness Act strengthens European competitiveness and the innovation capacity of the European game industry while maintaining strong consumer protection in the EU digital market?

Does the Commission see a role for pan-European co-regulation to ensure a fast and efficient response to sector-specific concerns, allowing the maintenance of a horizontal and principle-based consumer protection framework?

Will the Commission look at the how the enforcement of existing rules can be improved before devising new rules? The guidelines on Article 28 of the Digital Services Act2 already deal with commercial practices in games.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.3.2026) Consumer protection, competitiveness and sustainable prosperity are mutually reinforcing. The Digital Fairness Act (DFA) will aim to better protect consumers online by addressing identified consumer protection gaps, in full complementarity with existing legislation.

The ongoing impact assessment will examine different options, including if specific action is needed especially to protect minors. It will look into various approaches, including coregulation, to frame the possible measures. Enforcement of existing legislation is a key priority for the Commission. Investigatory and enforcement actions by the Commission are ongoing based on Article 28(1) of Regulation 2022/20651.
National Consumer Authorities, under the existing consumer legislation2, are also carrying out investigatory and enforcement actions3.

The Guidelines on the Protection of Minors4 offer a significant and meaningful benchmark on which the Commission will base itself when determining the compliance of providers of online platforms accessible to minors with Article 28 of Regulation 2022/20655 to provide a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors.

The Commission will pay particular attention at complementarity with the DFA and other relevant rules6. By clarifying consumer protection rules, it will facilitate enforcement and improve competitiveness through greater legal certainty, a more level playing field and more harmonisation for traders. It will also include simplification elements.
